content: Magnesium sulphate is the preferred medication for preventing and treating eclampsia in pregnant women. Over time, different regimens for administering this drug have been developed, but there is no definitive evidence to determine which regimen is superior in terms of benefits or risks. This review aimed to evaluate whether one magnesium sulphate regimen is more effective than another in reducing severe complications or death in women with pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, as well as in their babies. The review included 16 trials involving 3020 women. Four trials focused on women with eclampsia, while 12 trials addressed women with pre-eclampsia. Most of the studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries and had small sample sizes. Randomisation and allocation concealment were adequate in 11 trials, but blinding of participants and clinicians was generally not feasible. The risk of attrition and reporting bias was low in most studies. Treatment of Women with Eclampsia: 1. Loading Dose Alone vs. Loading Dose Plus Maintenance Dose: One trial with 80 women compared these regimens. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it remains unclear whether either regimen affects the risk of recurrent convulsions or maternal death. 2. Lower-Dose vs. Standard-Dose Regimen: A trial involving 72 women compared these regimens over 24 hours. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is uncertain whether either regimen impacts the risk of recurrent convulsions, severe complications, perinatal death, or maternal death. 3. Intravenous (IV) vs. Intramuscular (IM) Maintenance Regimen: One trial with 137 women compared these routes of administration. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether either route affects the recurrence of convulsions, stillbirths, neonatal deaths, or maternal deaths. 4. Short Maintenance Regimen vs. Standard 24-Hour Maintenance Regimen: A trial with 120 women compared these durations. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether the duration of maintenance therapy affects convulsion recurrence, severe complications, or side effects like nausea and respiratory failure. However, a short maintenance regimen may reduce the risk of flushing compared to the standard 24-hour regimen (low-certainty evidence). Prevention of Eclampsia in Women with Pre-Eclampsia: 1. Loading Dose Alone vs. Loading Dose Plus Maintenance Therapy: Two trials with 462 women compared these regimens. Low-certainty evidence suggests that the effect on the risk of eclampsia or perinatal death is uncertain. 2. IV vs. IM Maintenance Regimen: A small trial with 17 women compared these routes over 24 hours. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether either route affects the risk of eclampsia or stillbirth. 3. Short Postpartum Maintenance Regimen vs. 24-Hour Postpartum Maintenance Regimen: Four trials with 1713 women compared these durations. Low-certainty evidence suggests a wide range of possible benefits or harms regarding eclampsia. There may be little or no effect on severe complications or side effects like respiratory depression. 4. Higher-Dose vs. Lower-Dose Maintenance Regimen: Three trials with 185 women compared these regimens. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether either regimen affects the risk of eclampsia. Low-certainty evidence suggests that a higher-dose regimen has little or no effect on side effects compared to a lower-dose regimen. 5. Continuous Infusion vs. Serial IV Bolus Regimen: One trial with 200 women compared these methods of administration. The evidence was of very low certainty, and it is unclear whether the method of administration affects eclampsia, side effects, perinatal death, maternal death, or neonatal complications. Authors' Conclusions: Despite the number of trials conducted, there is no strong evidence to suggest that one magnesium sulphate regimen is more effective than another for the prevention or treatment of eclampsia. Further well-designed randomised controlled trials are necessary to address this question.
